1.pericope_label: Now when these things were done, the princes came to me, saying, The people of Israel, and the priests, and the Levites, have not separated themselves from the people of the lands, doing according to their abominations, even of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites. For they have taken of their daughters for themselves, and for their sons: so that the holy seed have mingled themselves with the people of those lands: yea, the hand of the princes and rulers hath been chief in this trespass. And when I heard this thing, I rent my garment and my mantle, and plucked off the hair of my head and of my beard, and sat down astonied. Then were assembled unto me every one that trembled at the words of the God of Israel, because of the transgression of those that had been carried away; and I sat astonied until the evening sacrifice.

schools.summary: Delitzsch sets the scene in the temple some time after Ezra's arrival, when the princes of the people brought him word, and reads the signs of grief with care: the tearing of both upper and under garments was a token of heartfelt and grievous affliction, while the plucking out of part of the hair was an expression of violent wrath and moral indignation and is not to be identified with the cutting of the hair in mourning. The word rendered astonied he glosses as desolate, rigid, stunned, without motion, and he notes that the sitting lasted until the time of the evening sacrifice, when Ezra rose from a mortification usually effected by fasting but here by sitting motionless in deep affliction of soul. He is careful about the grammar of the rising, too: the words do not mean that Ezra arose with his garments already torn, but that on arising he rent them afresh before falling on his knees and spreading out his hands.

Gill supplies the circumstances the narrative compresses. The report came after the returning captives had refreshed themselves, weighed out the money and vessels into the hands of the proper persons, offered their sacrifices and delivered the king's commissions to his lieutenants and governors; those who brought it were the princes of the people, who had kept their own integrity. He works out the arithmetic of the offence, that some who were widowers took wives of those nations for themselves and took them for their sons as well, while some who already had wives took heathen ones besides, and he describes the company that gathered to Ezra as men who had a reverence for the word of God and the things contained in it, who feared to break his laws and trembled at the judgments they apprehended would come upon transgressors.

Clarke is the hardest reader of the offence. He judges that the settlers who had returned with Zerubbabel and were found in the land had become little better than the Canaanite nations from whom God had commanded them to keep for ever separate, and he takes Ezra's mourning to testify abhorrence not merely of the taking of strange wives but of having joined those wives in their idolatrous abominations. On the phrase that the hand of the princes was chief in the trespass he comments on rank, that those who were the first men proved the most capital offenders, the first meaning the most illustrious, as we say the first men of the kingdom for the nobles. He adds that the rending of clothes was common to all ancient nations, that shaving the head and beard were signs of excessive grief and the plucking of hair much more so since it must produce exquisite pain, and that the morning sacrifice was the first offering of the day and the evening sacrifice the last, offered between sunset and the end of twilight. Wesley notes that the evening hour was when the people used to assemble together, and draws the application that all good people ought to own those who appear and act for God against vice and profaneness, every one who fears God doing what he can to strengthen their hands.

Henry lays four counts against the marriages: they disobeyed the express command forbidding all intimacy with the heathen and particularly in matrimonial contracts; they profaned the crown of their peculiarity by setting themselves level with those above whom God had lately dignified them; they distrusted his power to protect them and were led by carnal policy, hoping to strengthen themselves by making an interest among their neighbours, since a practical disbelief of God's all-sufficiency is at the bottom of all the sorry shifts we make to help ourselves; and they exposed their children to the very sin, introduced by this very way, that had once been the ruin of their church and nation. He is willing to hope they did not worship the gods of those lands, their captivity having cured them of idolatry. He presses that the guilty included priests and Levites whose office was to teach this law, and that the hand of the princes who should have prevented the trespass was chief in it, since princes in a trespass are charged as chief because of the influence of their example, and miserable is the people whose leaders debauch them. The information, he notes, came from the right quarter and to the right man, and those who cannot themselves reform public abuses may still serve by informing those who can.

debates: What the phrase about doing according to their abominations amounts to, where Henry restricts it to the imitation of the heathen in promiscuous marriages, which by degrees would lead to idolatry, while Clarke takes the mourning that follows as evidence that the Jews had already joined their wives in idolatrous worship.

What the signs of grief signify, where Delitzsch distinguishes the torn garments as affliction from the plucked hair as wrath and moral indignation, while Clarke treats both as degrees of excessive grief and measures the plucking by the pain it must produce.

Who is charged by the notice that the hand of the princes was chief in this trespass, which Henry reads as guilt multiplied by the force of a ruler's example, and Clarke as a comment on rank, the first men proving the most capital offenders.
outliers: Delitzsch notes that the Hebrew does not say Ezra arose with his garments already torn, but that he rent them again on rising.
Gill places the report after the whole business of the return had been discharged, the money and vessels weighed out and the king's commissions delivered.

5.pericope_label: And at the evening sacrifice I arose up from my heaviness; and having rent my garment and my mantle, I fell upon my knees, and spread out my hands unto the Lord my God, And said, O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God: for our iniquities are increased over our head, and our trespass is grown up unto the heavens. Since the days of our fathers have we been in a great trespass unto this day; and for our iniquities have we, our kings, and our priests, been delivered into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, and to a spoil, and to confusion of face, as it is this day. And now for a little space grace hath been shewed from the Lord our God, to leave us a remnant to escape, and to give us a nail in his holy place, that our God may lighten our eyes, and give us a little reviving in our bondage. For we were bondmen; yet our God hath not forsaken us in our bondage, but hath extended mercy unto us in the sight of the kings of Persia, to give us a reviving, to set up the house of our God, and to repair the desolations thereof, and to give us a wall in Judah and in Jerusalem. And now, O our God, what shall we say after this? for we have forsaken thy commandments, Which thou hast commanded by thy servants the prophets, saying, The land, unto which ye go to possess it, is an unclean land with the filthiness of the people of the lands, with their abominations, which have filled it from one end to another with their uncleanness. Now therefore give not your daughters unto their sons, neither take their daughters unto your sons, nor seek their peace or their wealth for ever: that ye may be strong, and eat the good of the land, and leave it for an inheritance to your children for ever. And after all that is come upon us for our evil deeds, and for our great trespass, seeing that thou our God hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve, and hast given us such deliverance as this; Should we again break thy commandments, and join in affinity with the people of these abominations? wouldest not thou be angry with us till thou hadst consumed us, so that there should be no remnant nor escaping? O Lord God of Israel, thou art righteous: for we remain yet escaped, as it is this day: behold, we are before thee in our trespasses: for we cannot stand before thee because of this.

schools.summary: Delitzsch lays out the train of thought in the prayer as a connected argument: Ezra scarcely dares lift up his face to God for shame at the greatness of their misdeeds; from the days of their fathers God has sorely punished them for their sins by delivering them into the power of their enemies; but he has now again turned his pity towards them and revived them in the place of his sanctuary through the favour of the king of Persia; and they have transgressed his commands afresh, the commands with whose keeping God had connected their possession of the good land. He identifies the little moment as the short interval between the release under Cyrus and the moment of speaking, set against the long period of suffering from the times of the Assyrians onward, and reads the question what shall we say after this as answerable only in one way, that they have forsaken his commandments and requited his kindness with sins. On the closing appeal he is exact: Ezra appeals to the righteousness of God not to supplicate pardon, as Nehemiah does elsewhere, for that righteousness would impel God to extirpate a sinful nation, but to rouse the conscience of the community.

Gill reads the prayer as an act of faith before it is an act of penitence: it opens with God addressed as a covenant God even as confession is about to be made, since the prayer that is right is the one put up in faith, and the repentance that is genuine is the one accompanied by faith and flowing from it. He notes what Ezra rose from, the signs of heaviness and particularly the sitting on the ground, or his fasting, since he had eaten nothing that day. On the aggravations he observes that the sins had been long continued in, which was itself an aggravation; that it was only a small time since the Lord first began to show them favour, so that their revolt argues a strange propensity of mind to evil which the recent goodness of God could not restrain; and that no apology or excuse can be made for such ingratitude. He grants the closing confession its full force, that God would appear righteous should Israel be entirely cut off and utterly consumed for their iniquities.

Clarke takes the posture for the deepest humility, the hands spread out as if to lay hold on the mercy of God, and makes the shame concrete: God had so often been provoked and had so often pardoned that Ezra was ashamed to go back again to the throne of grace to ask mercy on their behalf, which he calls the genuine feeling of every reawakened backslider. He glosses the nail in the holy place as even so much ground as to fix their tent-poles in, explains the lightening of the eyes as a thorough knowledge of themselves and of their highest interest, and reads the little reviving as a new trial granted to a people who were perishing and who, because of their sins, had been sentenced to death. On the last verse he argues that righteous here means merciful, one of the many meanings of the Hebrew word, which is why a remnant escaped at all, and adds that they had no righteousness but stood clothed and covered with their trespasses. Wesley agrees about the hour and the type, has Ezra include himself because he was guilty of many sins and because the guilt had by now become national, takes the nail for some kind of settlement on the figure of tents fastened with cords and pins, and answers the policy behind the marriages directly: they may fancy that leagues and marriages are the only way to establish them, but it will weaken and ruin them, and the contrary course will make them strong.

Henry makes the hour part of the meaning. Devout people used to come into the courts at the evening sacrifice, and in their hearing Ezra chose to make this confession so that they might be made sensible of the sins of their people, which hitherto they had either not noticed or had made light of: prayer may preach. The sacrifice was itself a type of the great propitiation, the Lamb who in the evening of the world was to take away sin by the sacrifice of himself, so that Ezra confesses with his hand as it were upon the head of that sacrifice. He observes that what follows is not properly a prayer, since there is not a word of petition in it, but the offering up of devout affections, a lively picture of ingenuous repentance; and that Ezra, though wholly clear of this guilt, puts himself among the sinners as a member of the same community, perhaps remembering against himself that he had stayed so long after his brethren in Babylon. He then follows the aggravations one by one: iniquities increased over their heads so that they are ready to perish as in deep waters and grown up to the heavens, where nevertheless God's mercy also is; a sin long persisted in, the fathers' example aggravating rather than excusing it; judgments already suffered without reformation, brayed in the mortar and the folly not gone; mercies lately received and ill requited; an express command broken, since sin appears exceedingly sinful when compared with the law it breaks; and a punishment lighter than their iniquities deserved, so that they stood still in debt on the old account and were now running up a new score.

debates: What the appeal to God's righteousness is for, where Delitzsch insists it is not a plea for pardon, since righteousness would require the extirpation of a sinful nation, but a summons to the conscience of the community, while Clarke reads righteous as merciful and makes that very righteousness the reason a remnant escaped.

Why Ezra says our sins when he is clear of the guilt, where Henry takes it as a member owning the sin of his community, with perhaps a glance at his own delay in Babylon, and Wesley as a plain confession that he too was guilty of many sins and that the guilt had become national.

What the nail in his holy place means, which Clarke reduces to so much ground as to fix a tent-pole in, Wesley takes for a settlement on the same figure of tents and cords, and Henry expands into the house of God set up and the temple service running in a constant method.
outliers: Clarke calls Ezra's reluctance to return to the throne of grace the genuine feeling of every reawakened backslider.
Henry observes that though their iniquities reached to the heavens, God's mercy is in the heavens too, so that where sin abounds grace much more abounds.
